Concrete sealing, and how to tell if you need it

Paths, alfresco areas, patios, porches, garage floors and slabs across Melbourne. Before anyone quotes you, tip a cup of water on the surface. If it beads, you are already sealed and you do not need us. If it soaks straight in and darkens, the concrete is drinking everything that lands on it.

  • Penetrating or topical, your choice
  • Needs two to three clear days after cleaning
  • Quoted per square metre, separately from cleaning
Get A Quote 0400 638 010

Do it yourself first

The water drop test. Pour a cup of water onto the concrete and wait thirty seconds. If it sits up in a bead, there is a working sealer on it and nothing needs doing. If it spreads and the concrete goes dark underneath it, the surface is porous and open.

That single test answers the question most quotes dance around, and it is also how you know when a sealer has reached the end of its life. A penetrating sealer gives no visual warning at all: it does not peel or dull, it just quietly stops repelling. Checking once a year with a cup of water is the entire maintenance schedule.

Penetrating or topical

Two very different answers

This page covers concrete that is not a driveway. Driveways take traffic, turning and hot tyres, which changes the recommendation, so they have their own page.

Both are legitimate. The choice is mostly about whether you want the concrete to look different afterwards.
  Penetrating Topical
Where it sits Inside the capillaries, below the surface As a film on top of the surface
How it looks Identical to before. Nobody can tell it has been done Satin to gloss. Colours deepen as if permanently wet
Service life Five to seven years Three to five years
When it wears out Silently. Only the water test tells you Visibly. The sheen dulls and patches appear
Reapplying Clean and recoat. Nothing to strip Usually needs the old coat removed if it has failed
Slip No change to the surface texture at all Can be slippery wet unless an anti slip additive is used
Best for Paths, porches and anywhere you want no visual change Alfresco, patios and decorative concrete where the look is the point

Swipe for the rest of the columns

Where it earns its money

Concrete surfaces other than the driveway

Alfresco and patios

Food, drink, barbecue fat and sunscreen all stain unsealed concrete and all of it wipes off a sealed one. The surface most people regret not sealing.

Front paths and porches

Usually shaded, so they grow faster than anything else. Sealed, there is nowhere for the growth to get a hold.

Pool surrounds

Permanently damp, with chlorinated splash. Sealed with an anti slip additive is the standard answer here. Anti slip sealing.

Garage floors

Where oil drips, tyre marks and dropped tools live. A sealed garage floor is the difference between sweeping and scrubbing.

New slabs

The best time to seal anything, because nothing has stained it yet. Wait for the concrete to cure first, which is around twenty eight days.

Commercial walkways and entries

High traffic, high visibility, and far cheaper to maintain sealed than to clean repeatedly. Quoted through commercial exterior cleaning.

The sequence

Why it is never same day

STEP 01

Clean, and finish cleaning

Every stain out, because sealing over one locks it in permanently. This is where the decision about what is coming out and what is not gets made.

STEP 02

Dry right through

Two to three clear days in a Melbourne summer, longer through winter. Not touch dry: dry through the slab. A topical sealer over trapped moisture goes milky white and has to be stripped.

STEP 03

Test the porosity

The water drop test again, plus a check for anything applied previously that would stop a new coat bonding.

STEP 04

Two coats, then cure

The second goes on once the first has pulled in. Foot traffic after a day, nothing heavy for three, and no sharp turning for a week.

Questions

Asked about sealing concrete

How long will the sealer last?

Between about two and ten years, and the spread is that wide because it depends on the product, the preparation, which way the slab faces and whether a car parks on it.

It also fails gradually rather than suddenly, which is why testing it with a glass of water matters. How long concrete sealing lasts goes through all of it.

How do I know if my concrete is already sealed?

Tip a cup of water on it and wait half a minute. Beading means a working sealer. Soaking in and darkening means it is open and porous.

Do it in two or three places, because sealers wear out unevenly. The track where people walk usually goes first while the edges are still beading.

How long does concrete sealing last?

Five to seven years for a penetrating sealer on a path or patio, three to five for a topical system. Less under vehicle traffic, which is why driveways are a separate conversation.

Shade, exposure and how much the surface is used move it more than the product does.

Will sealing change how my concrete looks?

A penetrating sealer does not change it at all, which is the point of it. A topical sealer very much does: it deepens the colour and adds a satin or gloss sheen, so the concrete looks permanently like it does just after rain.

Plenty of people want that and plenty do not. It is worth seeing a sample before deciding, and we will do a test area so you can look at it dry.

Can you seal concrete that has stains in it?

You can, and you should not. Whatever is visible when the sealer goes on is permanent for the life of the coating, and getting at it afterwards means stripping the sealer first.

Stain work comes before sealing, always. Where a mark is not going to come out completely, that is a conversation to have before the sealer rather than after.

What happens if you seal damp concrete?

With a topical sealer, the trapped moisture turns it milky white. It cannot be polished out or rescued. The coating has to be stripped and the job done again, which is why we will not seal on a schedule that does not allow proper drying.

A penetrating sealer is more forgiving but still works poorly on a damp slab, because the capillaries it needs to get into are already full.

Is it worth sealing a new slab?

It is the best time there is, because nothing has stained it yet and you are protecting a clean surface rather than preserving a cleaned one.

Wait for the concrete to cure first, around twenty eight days, and let any efflorescence finish coming out. Sealing too early traps curing moisture.
